Philadelphia Flyers :: History :: Broad Street Bullies (1971–1981) :: 1974–75 Stanley Cup champions :: part 01 :: chunk_0007
Under the [1974–75 season](/wiki/1974%E2%80%9375_NHL_season "1974–75 NHL season"), Dave Schultz topped his mark from the previous season by setting an NHL record for penalty minutes with 472. Clarke's efforts earned him his second Hart Trophy and Parent was the lone recipient of the Vezina Trophy. The Flyers as a team improved their record slightly with a mark of 51–18–11, the best record in the NHL. After a first-round bye, the Flyers easily swept the Toronto Maple Leafs and were presented with another New York-area team in the semifinals, the [New York Islanders](/wiki/New_York_Islanders "New York Islanders"). The Flyers looked to be headed toward another sweep after winning the first three games. However, the Islanders fought back by winning the next three games, setting up a deciding seventh game. The Flyers were finally able to shut the door on the Islanders, winning game seven, 4–1.

Facing Buffalo in the [Stanley Cup Final](/wiki/1975_Stanley_Cup_Final "1975 Stanley Cup Final"), the Flyers won the first two games at home. Game three, played in Buffalo, went down in hockey lore as "The Fog Game" due to an unusual May heatwave in Buffalo that forced parts of the game to be played in heavy fog, as Buffalo's arena lacked air conditioning. The Flyers lost games 3 and 4, but won game five at home in dominating fashion, 5–1. On the road for game six, [Bob Kelly](/wiki/Bob_Kelly_(ice_hockey,_born_1950) "Bob Kelly (ice hockey, born 1950)") scored the decisive goal and Parent pitched another shutout (a playoff record fifth shutout) as the Flyers repeated as Stanley Cup champions. Parent also repeated as the playoffs MVP, winning a second consecutive Conn Smythe Trophy.

Esther Duflo was awarded the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel in 2019 along with her two co-researchers Abhijit Banerjee and Michael Kremer "for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty". Duflo is the youngest person (at age 46) and the second woman to win this award (after [Elinor Ostrom](/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom "Elinor Ostrom") in 2009).[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37)

The press release from the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") noted: "Their experimental research methods now entirely dominate [development economics](/wiki/Development_economics "Development economics")."[[38]](#cite_note-NobelWeb-38)[[39]](#cite_note-guardianlive-39) The Nobel committee commented:

> Banerjee, Duflo and their co-authors concluded that students appeared to learn nothing from additional days at school. Neither did spending on textbooks seem to boost learning, even though the schools in Kenya lacked many essential inputs. Moreover, in the Indian context Banerjee and Duflo intended to study, many children appeared to learn little: in results from field tests in the city of [Vadodara](/wiki/Vadodara "Vadodara") fewer than one in five third-grade students could correctly answer first-grade curriculum math test questions.[[39]](#cite_note-guardianlive-39)

> In response to such findings, Banerjee, Duflo and co-authors argued that efforts to get more children into school must be complemented by reforms to improve school quality.[[39]](#cite_note-guardianlive-39)

The Packers have been league champions a record 13 times,[[25]](#cite_note-championships-26) topping their nearest rival, the Chicago Bears, by four. The first three were decided by league standing, the next six by the [NFL Title Game](/wiki/History_of_National_Football_League_Championship "History of National Football League Championship"), and the last four by [Super Bowl](/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") victories. The Packers are also the only team to win three consecutive NFL titles, having accomplished this twice—from 1929 to 1931 under Lambeau, and from 1965 to 1967 under Lombardi.

*Oppenheimer* earned a leading 13 nominations at the [96th Academy Awards](/wiki/96th_Academy_Awards "96th Academy Awards"), becoming Nolan's most Oscar-nominated film.[[294]](#cite_note-298)[[295]](#cite_note-299)[[296]](#cite_note-300) At the ceremony, the film won [Best Picture](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), [Best Director](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director"), [Best Actor](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for Murphy, [Best Supporting Actor](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor") for Downey Jr., [Best Cinematography](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Cinematography "Academy Award for Best Cinematography"), [Best Film Editing](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Film_Editing "Academy Award for Best Film Editing"), and [Best Original Score](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Academy Award for Best Original Score").[[103]](#cite_note-:0-104) Besides composer Göransson, all recipients were first-time Oscar winners, including Nolan, Thomas, Roven, Downey Jr. and van Hoytema, who had each earned previous Academy Award nominations.[[297]](#cite_note-301) *Oppenheimer* became both the highest-grossing and longest Best Picture winning film since 2003's *[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King](/wiki/The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Return_of_the_King "The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King")*.[[298]](#cite_note-302) The film was also nominated for [Best Supporting Actress](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") for Blunt, [Best Adapted Screenplay](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay"

Among mammalian prey species, [bats](/wiki/Bat "Bat") in the genera *[Eptesicus](/wiki/Eptesicus "Eptesicus")*, *[Myotis](/wiki/Myotis "Myotis")*, *[Pipistrellus](/wiki/Pipistrellus "Pipistrellus")* and *[Tadarida](/wiki/Tadarida "Tadarida")* are the most common prey taken at night.[[77]](#cite_note-82) Though peregrines generally do not prefer terrestrial mammalian prey, in [Rankin Inlet](/wiki/Rankin_Inlet "Rankin Inlet"), peregrines largely take [northern collared lemmings](/wiki/Northern_collared_lemming "Northern collared lemming") (*Dicrostonyx groenlandicus*) along with a few [Arctic ground squirrels](/wiki/Arctic_ground_squirrel "Arctic ground squirrel") (*Urocitellus parryii*).[[78]](#cite_note-83) Other small mammals including [shrews](/wiki/Shrew "Shrew"), [mice](/wiki/Mouse "Mouse"), [rats](/wiki/Rat "Rat"), [voles](/wiki/Vole "Vole"), and [squirrels](/wiki/Squirrel "Squirrel") are more seldom taken.[[74]](#cite_note-Drewitt2008-79)[[79]](#cite_note-Ratcliffe-84) Peregrines occasionally take [rabbits](/wiki/Rabbit "Rabbit"), mainly young individuals and juvenile [hares](/wiki/Hare "Hare").[[79]](#cite_note-Ratcliffe-84)[[80]](#cite_note-Pagel.-85) Additionally, remains of [red fox](/wiki/Red_fox "Red fox") kits and adult female [American marten](/wiki/American_marten "American marten") were found among prey remains.[[80]](#cite_note-Pagel.-85) Insects and reptiles such as small [snakes](/wiki/Snake "Snake") make up a small proportion of the diet, and [salmonid fish](/wiki/Salmonidae "Salmonidae") have been taken by peregrines.[[18]](#cite_note-Beckstead2001-18)[[79]](#cite_note-Ratcliffe-84)[[81]](#cite_note-86)

The five-story base as seen from Fifth Avenue, with the main entrance at center. The Empire State Building sets back significantly above the base.

The Empire State Building has a symmetrical [massing](/wiki/Massing "Massing") because of its large lot and relatively short base. Its [articulation](/wiki/Articulation_(architecture) "Articulation (architecture)") consists of three horizontal sections—a base, shaft, and [capital](/wiki/Capital_(architecture) "Capital (architecture)")—similar to the components of a [column](/wiki/Column "Column").[[33]](#cite_note-Reynolds_p._290-36) The five-story base occupies the entire lot, while the 81-story shaft above it is [set back](/wiki/Setback_(architecture) "Setback (architecture)") sharply from the base.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESternGilmartinMellins1987612-39)[[37]](#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1930a-40)[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELandmarks_Preservation_Commission198115-41) The setback above the 5th story is 60 feet (18 m) deep on all sides.[[33]](#cite_note-Reynolds_p._290-36) There are also setbacks at the 21st, 25th, 30th, 72nd, 81st, and 85th stories,[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELandmarks_Preservation_Commission198116-42) positioning these floors away from the noisy streets below.[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETauranac2014157-43)[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaydenMunicipal_Art_Society20008–9-44) The setbacks correspond to the tops of elevator shafts, allowing interior spaces to be at most 28 feet (8.5 m) deep (see: [§ Interior](#Interior)).[[33]](#cite_note-Reynolds_p._290-36)

The setbacks were mandated by the [1916 Zoning Resolution](/wiki/1916_Zoning_Resolution "1916 Zoning Resolution"), which was intended to allow sunlight to reach the streets as well.[[d]](#

On July 13, 2022, Ono was named as the [15th president](/wiki/President_of_the_University_of_Michigan "President of the University of Michigan") of the [University of Michigan](/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan"), with his term beginning on October 13, 2022.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38) He became the first Japanese-American to lead the university. In October 2023, Ono received a 4% raise in base salary, increasing it from US$975,000 to US$1,014,000 annually.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

Under the Ono presidency, the university conducted a renovation of the [President's House](/wiki/President%27s_House,_University_of_Michigan "President's House, University of Michigan"), the official residence of the university president, from 2022 to 2023 at a cost of US$11.5 million.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

During Ono's March 2023 address, he stated that DEI would be a major focus of his presidency.[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-42) In response to a donor's request for clarification on how the university spent money on DEI programs in 2023, Ono wrote, "I'm very proud of what has been accomplished and I'm excited about what's going to happen with DEI 2.0".[[43]](#cite_note-43) In January 2024, the university was reported to have 241 employees in the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) offices, with payroll costs totaling more than US$30 million annually.[[44]](#cite_note-44) On March 27, 2025, citing the [Trump administration's](/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump") executive order, Ono reversed his previous DEI policies and shut down the university's DEI programs and offices.[[45]](#cite_note-45)[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-47)

The **Sahara** ([/səˈhɑːrə/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), [/səˈhɛrə/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) is a [desert](/wiki/Desert "Desert") spanning [North Africa](/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa"). With an area of 9,200,000 square kilometres (3,600,000 sq mi), it is the largest hot desert in the world and the [third-largest desert](/wiki/List_of_deserts_by_area "List of deserts by area") overall, smaller only than the deserts of [Antarctica](/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica") and the northern [Arctic](/wiki/Arctic "Arctic").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-geology.com-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Size_and_Population_of_Sahara-4)
